summary: Deep technical discussion about tradeoffs of where to place safety filters and moderation checks to minimize latency and cost while preserving reliability and auditability. Reviewed inline vs out-of-band moderation, batching/kv-cache impacts, quantization profiling, and private deployment constraints for regulated PHI workloads.
topics: moderation placement: inline vs sidecar vs separate service
latency overhead of filters and batching strategies
KV cache and prefix caching interaction with moderation
VPC/on-prem implications for moderation and audit logs
fallbacks and graceful degradation for high-latency checks
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-16 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~66 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Eli (Redwood SE), Samira (Redwood SE), Carlos (Novus Head of ML), Priya (Novus Security), Leo (Novus SRE), Aisha (Novus PM)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we wanted to focus today on guardrails specifically the moderation pipeline and where to place checks so you can meet Novus's latency SLAs and compliance needs. quick intro round?
[00:18] Carlos: yeah thanks Maya. I'm Carlos, I run ML at Novus. main constraint is we serve patient-facing features, so PHI considerations, also we have a 300ms p95 latency goal for suggestion endpoints.
[00:30] Maya: got it. Eli do you want to frame the options?
[00:35] Eli: sure. so broadly there are three architectural patterns we see: first, inline filtering — the model output is sent through a lightweight classifier synchronously before returning. second, sidecar/out-of-band — you return the primary response and run heavier moderation async, optionally revoking or flagging content. third, pre-filtering at the prompt level — detect risky prompts early and block or route to dedicated infra. each has tradeoffs on latency, cost, and auditability.
[01:12] Priya: can you quantify the latency impact for inline? like if we add a safety classifier after a 50ms generation.
[01:20] Eli: yes rough numbers from our benchmarks: a small binary classifier (quantized int8) on a small GPU or CPU can add 10-40ms when batched well; a heavier transformer-based classifier can be 80-200ms. but that depends on batching, sequence length, and whether it's colocated on the same instance as the generator.
[01:40] Leo: so batching helps but our p95 is tight — how does Redwood's KV cache/batching interact with inline checks?
[01:48] Samira: good question. KV cache speedups primarily benefit autoregressive decoding for repeated prefixes; moderation checks typically operate on the final decoded string or on logits/hidden states. If you do classification on logits early you can sometimes avoid full decode but that needs a classifier trained on logits and we don't enable that by default. The practical pattern is: continue to use KV cache for generation, then run classifier on the final output; you can batch many final outputs to amortize cost, but that introduces tail latency for some users unless you use adaptive batching.
[02:25] Aisha: adaptive batching?
[02:27] Eli: yeah, Redwood's runtime supports latency buckets — small requests can be prioritized for immediate processing while lower priority ones wait up to X ms for batch fill. You can configure a strict SLO for sensitive routes so they bypass batch windows.
[02:40] Carlos: we heard about doing moderation inside the model — like instruction-tuned models with guardrail behavior — any thoughts?
[02:47] Eli: in-model safety reduces external pipeline complexity but it's brittle for policy updates and auditing. Also it's tough to prove absence of unsafe outputs; for compliance teams they prefer deterministic filters and auditable decision logs. So often we do hybrid: model-level steering + an external classifier for enforcement and logging.
[03:05] Priya: audit logs are a hard requirement for us. must keep hashes of inputs/outputs and policy decisions for 7 years. can Redwood capture that in VPC/private?
[03:14] Maya: yes, in Private deployments logs can be customer-controlled. we can surface decision logs, classifier confidence, and policy tag metadata, and integrate with your KMS so you keep the keys. We'll include SOC2 docs.
[03:26] Leo: how much does the classifier confidence scoring add to token cost and latency?
[03:31] Eli: negligible token cost if classifier is separate; compute cost is the main factor. For small models we typically quantize to int8 and run on CPU or smaller GPUs which greatly reduces cost. But quantization can slightly change classifier accuracy — we recommend running evals on your labeled set to estimate delta.
[03:48] Carlos: could quantization make us miss PHI mentions? risk is false negatives.
[03:53] Samira: that's why benchmarking with your data is critical. we've seen 1-3% AUC drop moving from float16 to int8 for certain architectures; in practice if you cascade (e.g., int8 fast pass + float16 fallback for low confidence) you can get both speed and safety.
[04:12] Aisha: explain cascade pattern, please.
[04:15] Eli: simple: run a fast quantized classifier inline and if confidence is high -> accept. If confidence is low or flagged -> route to a heavier classifier or human review. You can tune thresholds to balance cost and recall. For latency sensitive routes, you might return a safe fallback while heavier checks run asynchronously and then notify/rollback if needed.
[04:40] Priya: async rollback seems tricky for UX — how do customers handle removal of content after it's visible to users?
[04:47] Samira: common approach is shadow moderation for a trial period to measure false positives/negatives, and design UX for edits or take-downs — e.g., show a provisional label or disable actions until verification. For critical PHI exposures we prefer to block synchronously.
[05:05] Carlos: metrics — what should we track?
[05:08] Eli: track latency p50/p95 for generation and moderation, classifier throughput, false positive/negative rates, confidence distribution, and rollback frequency. Also cost per 1k requests for each pipeline variant.
[05:22] Carlos: ok. let's talk placement cost comparison — inline vs sidecar.
[05:26] Eli: inline (colocated) classifier co-hosted on the same GPU instance as generation reduces network hop but competes for memory/compute; on smaller instances that can increase generation latency. Sidecar (separate service) isolates resources, allows independent scaling and different hardware (CPU for classifier), and simplifies auditing. Sidecar adds RPC overhead (1-5ms on same AZ, more across regions) but you gain operational flexibility.
[05:52] Leo: does Redwood support running classifier as CPU-only on sidecars in private deployments?
[05:56] Maya: yes, in Private you can select instance types — classifier sidecars on CPU nodes, generator on GPU nodes. Redwood's runtime can handle the routing and metrics aggregation.
[06:06] Priya: what about batching across services? if generator batches and sidecar batches separately, does that harm ordering?
[06:12] Eli: it can complicate latency predictability. We implement per-request IDs and re-order tolerant pipelines; but if you batch too long at either stage you get cross-stage tail effects. We advise aligning max wait windows and using small batch sizes for high priority traffic.
[06:30] Carlos: any guidance for quantization selection? int8 vs int4?
[06:33] Samira: int8 is the pragmatic sweet spot for classifiers and many generator models: good speedup with modest accuracy impact. int4 is more aggressive and often needs specialized kernels and can degrade behavior for certain sensitive detection tasks. If you use int4, always run evals and consider float16 fallback for low-confidence cases.
[06:53] Aisha: can we cache moderation decisions? like if the same prompt-output pair appears again?
[06:57] Eli: yes, caching decisions keyed on prompt hash + output hash is effective. Redwood's KV store can persist small decision caches and TTL them. That reduces repeated classifier runs for high-frequency queries. Caveat: if policy changes you must invalidate cache or store policy version in the key.
[07:18] Priya: and metadata — we need to keep policy version in audit logs.
[07:21] Maya: agreed; we include policy version, classifier model version, confidence, and hash keys in the log.
[07:28] Carlos: what about placement when using on-prem or VPC? latency within customer's network might be variable.
[07:34] Eli: inside VPC you avoid public network overhead but you're bound to customer's hw. For on-prem with constrained GPU capacity, you might prefer sidecar CPU classifiers. Redwood can orchestrate fallback to Redwood-hosted classifiers for high-load conditions if you allow cross-connects; otherwise you should provision dedicated classifiers for peak.
[07:56] Leo: fallback to Redwood-hosted classifiers is a no-go for some regulated patients.
[07:59] Priya: correct, can't exfiltrate PHI.
[08:02] Maya: in that case all moderation must run inside your VPC/on-prem. Redwood can deliver Private deployments with customer-controlled logs and KMS so nothing leaves your environment. We also support running classifier bundles as part of the on-prem package.
[08:17] Carlos: let's talk numbers — can you run a small benchmark during the POC showing p95 impact for the three patterns?
[08:23] Eli: yes we propose running: baseline generation-only, generation + inline fast quantized classifier, generation + sidecar CPU classifier, and cascade (fast pass + heavy fallback). We'll run with your 1k-sample prompt set and measure p50/p95, throughput, and cost.
[08:36] Maya: we'll also test with KV cache on and off to show differences.
[08:40] Carlos: one more question on training classifiers — we have internal labels for PHI and abuse. Do you advise using Redwood's curated safety models or bringing own classifiers?
[08:50] Samira: both options supported. You can use Redwood's verified classifiers for common categories to bootstrap, then bring a custom model fine-tuned on your labeled set for final enforcement. We recommend ensembling: Redwood model for recall + custom model for precision.
[09:05] Priya: what's the overhead for ensembling?
[09:08] Eli: similar to cascade: you run a fast public model, then your custom model on low-confidence cases. Cost is dominated by the heavier model runs, so threshold tuning is key.
[09:18] Carlos: about testing how moderation works with function-calling and structured outputs — does that change placement?
[09:24] Samira: for structured outputs, you can validate schema on the client or server and run classifiers on either the structured fields or the raw text. If function calling yields sensitive fields, it's often best to run synchronous checks on the structured payload before invoking downstream systems. That keeps auditability strong.
[09:42] Aisha: any gotchas with streaming responses and moderation? like we stream partial tokens but we need to block if final output is unsafe.
[09:51] Eli: streaming complicates synchronous blocking. Approaches: hold the stream until classifier finishes (adds latency), stream low-risk tokens and stall/replace later segments, or stream but include strong disclaimers and run immediate follow-up moderation + retract if needed. Most customers prefer buffering critical routes until classification completes.
[10:12] Carlos: okay useful. how do you recommend setting thresholds during POC?
[10:16] Eli: pick conservative thresholds for recall during initial POC (fewer false negatives), measure false positives, then tune to cost/UX tradeoffs. Use seeded test cases and blind evals; track business impact metrics.
[10:29] Priya: we need to ensure we can capture decision provenance for audits. Can Redwood store immutable logs with HMAC or signatures?
[10:36] Maya: yes we can include signed logs using your KMS and provide an append-only store option in Private deployments.
[10:44] Leo: any recommended infra sizing for 300ms p95 and 2k qps peaks?
[10:49] Eli: depends on model size and classifier choice; as a ballpark for a medium LLM (7-13B) with KV cache and int8 classifier sidecar, estimate 4-6 GPU instances for generation + autoscaled CPU pool for classifiers. We'll model costs after we see your sample traffic profile.
[11:10] Carlos: let's capture acceptance criteria: how will Novus decide success of POC?
[11:14] Aisha: 1) p95 under 350ms for high-priority route with synchronous classification, 2) <2% false negatives for PHI detection on our labeled set, 3) audit logs contain policy/classifier version and hashes, and 4) acceptable cost per 1k requests.
[11:32] Maya: great. we'll draft an experiment plan and share it.
[11:36] Eli: quick note on eval harness — we can run experiments with different quantization settings and cascading thresholds and produce an ROC curve per configuration.
[11:44] Carlos: that would help.
[11:46] Priya: last question: how do you handle model upgrades changing classifier behavior? policy drift is a risk.
[11:53] Samira: version everything. Redwood supports model pinning and rollout policies. When you upgrade, run canary tests against your labeled prompts, compare metrics, and block rollout if regressions exceed thresholds. Also keep previous model binary for quick rollback.
[12:10] Maya: okay i'm going to summarize next steps and action items.
[12:14] Maya: Redwood will run the moderation benchmark with your sample payloads (Maya/Eli). We'll share SOC2 and architecture docs (Maya). Novus will provide anonymized prompt sets and label guide (Carlos). We tentatively schedule on-prem feasibility the week of 7/28 (Maya to schedule).
[12:31] Carlos: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[12:33] Aisha: thanks all.
